newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Netanyahu fights for political life.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Netanyahu fights for political life.

text.p: Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is fighting for his political life in the face of police accusations he broke the law.
Television stations sent shockwaves through the country with the news on Wednesday night that police wanted him charged in an influence-peddling scandal.
The 47-year-old Netanyahu, admired by supporters for his fluency before the cameras, had nothing to say this time. But a spokesman for the Israeli leader rushed to his defence.
"I have no doubt, no doubt whatsoever, that the prime minister has no problem with this affair -- that he will emerge completely clean," Shai Bazak told Channel One television.
The news was certain to hamper efforts by U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross to save Israel-PLO peacemaking -- even though Ross himself said the affair was none of his business.
Labour party leader Shimon Peres -- defeated by Netanyahu last May by fewer than 30,000 votes -- called the news a "political earthquake".
But with several "ifs" yet to be addressed, it was by no means clear whether Netanyahu would be charged or forced to resign in the scandal over a political appointment.
A cabinet minister close to Netanyahu, Yehoshua Matza, said the Likud party leader might have to call an election if the present attorney general decided to prosecute.
Prosecutors could still ignore the police recommendations to charge Netanyahu with fraud and breach of trust for appointing Roni Bar-On as attorney general in January.
Israel's Channel One has been alleging ever since that a Netanyahu ally on trial for corruption, politician Aryeh Deri, pushed Bar-On for the job in the hope of winning a plea bargain.
The television said Deri had promised that in return, his Shas party would support Netanyahu's deal with the Palestinians to redeploy in the West Bank town of Hebron.
Police acknowledged basing their recommendation on the testimony of a single witness and that defence attorneys might argue he was unreliable and perhaps an interested party.
Israeli radio stations said the witness was himself once tipped as a leading candidate for the job that went briefly to Bar-On.
Israel's Police Chief Assaf Hefetz told reporters: "In principle the text is that there is evidence for bringing an indictment against the prime minister on the charge of fraud and breach of trust."
Police had been under orders to keep the findings of their 995-page report under wraps pending a decision by early next week on whether to prosecute Netanyahu and three associates.
Netanyahu's lawyer Yaacov Weinroth called the charges "baseless".
He said police had in any event qualified their recommendation by saying Netanyahu -- already interrogated once for several hours -- would have to be questioned again.
Deri, who saw Netanyahu late on Wednesday, told reporters: "I can only tell you the prime minister is calm, strong, quite happy and I am convinced the matter will come to a swift end."
But outside the prime minister's Jerusalem house, some 50 protesters called Netanyahu by his nickname, chanting: "Bibi Go Home" and "Elections Now."
